text: The regulation defines a 'deep fake' as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1].

The Act defines AI literacy as skills, knowledge, and understanding that enable providers, deployers, and affected persons to make informed deployments of AI systems while gaining awareness of its opportunities, risks, and possible harms [1]. This definition applies when considering the respective rights and obligations of these parties within the context of the Regulation [1]. The obligation to support AI literacy does not require guaranteeing any specific level of literacy for any individual [2]. The Board may adopt recommendations to support the promotion of AI literacy based on European competence frameworks [2]. Codes of conduct may also include promoting AI literacy as a specific objective for voluntary application [5].

A small mid-cap enterprise (SMC) is defined in the AI Act as a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (2) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 [1]. The Regulation also refers to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as defined in Article 2 of the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC [2]. These categories are mentioned in the context of supporting innovation and avoiding unnecessary burdens for providers [3][4][5].

A change to an AI system is a "substantial modification" if it occurs after the system is placed on the market or put into service and was not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment [1]. This definition applies when the change affects the system's compliance with requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 or modifies its intended purpose [1]. Changes that are pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial assessment and included in the technical documentation do not count as substantial modifications [2]. If a distributor, importer, or deployer makes a substantial modification, they may be considered a provider subject to specific obligations [3]. The exact date for applying these rules to systems already on the market depends on whether they undergo significant design changes after the date of application of Chapter III [5].

The AI Office is defined as the Commission's function of contributing to the implementation, monitoring, and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, as well as AI governance [1]. It is tasked with developing Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI [3]. The Office may invite providers of general-purpose AI models and relevant stakeholders to participate in drawing up codes of practice [4]. Additionally, the AI Office has supervisory and enforcement powers, including the ability to conduct on-site inspections with assistance from national authorities [5].

No, the AI Act does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes. This exemption applies regardless of whether the systems are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification in the Union. The regulation explicitly states that this exclusion applies regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [1].

AI systems released under free and open-source licences are generally exempt from the Regulation, but this exemption has specific conditions. The Regulation does not apply to such systems unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or fall under Article 5 or 50 [1]. For general-purpose AI models, the obligations in Article 53 and 54 do not apply if the model is released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, unless the model presents systemic risks [2][3]. However, this exemption does not cover third parties supplying components for high-risk AI systems under a free and open-source licence [4]. Additionally, the Regulation excludes research, testing, or development activities prior to placing a system on the market or putting it into service [5].

No, an AI model built solely for scientific research and development is not covered by this Regulation. Article 2(6) explicitly states that the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Additionally, Article 2(8) excludes research, testing, or development activities regarding AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. However, testing in real-world conditions is not covered by this exclusion.

Yes, the AI Act applies to your company because the output of your AI system is used in the Union. This applies even though your company is established outside the EU, as the Regulation covers providers and deployers from third countries where the output is used in the Union. The Act applies to such entities regardless of whether they are established within the Union or in a third country. [4]

Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy for their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of these systems [1]. These measures must consider the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of the individuals, as well as the context in which the AI systems are used [1]. The obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for any individual [1]. The Commission and Member States are also required to support and facilitate the efforts of providers and deployers, particularly SMEs, in fulfilling this obligation [1]. The Board may adopt recommendations to support the promotion of AI literacy required under this article [3].

People overseeing a high-risk AI system must be able to properly understand its capacities and limitations and monitor its operation to detect anomalies [2]. They must remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the system's output, and decide when not to use it or to override its results [2]. Additionally, they must be able to intervene in or interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or similar procedure to bring it to a safe halt [2]. For certain systems, no action or decision based on the system's identification can be taken unless verified and confirmed by at least two competent natural persons [5]. These oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks and context of use of the system [4].

The provider must keep the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [1]. This documentation must be kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for that entire period [1]. The provider is also required to keep the EU declaration of conformity up-to-date as appropriate [3]. Additionally, the provider must submit a copy of the declaration to relevant national competent authorities upon request [1].

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database [1][2]. This registration requirement applies to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, excluding those in point 2 of that annex [1]. It also applies to AI systems where the provider has concluded they are not high-risk according to Article 6(3) [2]. Importers must verify that the provider has drawn up the EU declaration of conformity and appointed an authorised representative before placing the system on the market, but the registration obligation falls on the provider [5].

Yes, as an employer you must inform workers' representatives and affected workers before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace [1]. This information must be provided in accordance with Union and national law rules on informing workers [1]. The AI system must also be classified as high-risk under Annex III to trigger these obligations [2]. You are not required to test the system yourself, but the provider must ensure testing is performed prior to use [4]. If the system is used by a public authority, additional registration obligations apply [5].

Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment. Additionally, deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III are required to perform this assessment. This obligation applies to high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), with an exception for systems intended for use in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III. The assessment must include measures for internal governance and complaint mechanisms if risks materialize. [5]

A fundamental rights impact assessment must include the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by the system's use in the specific context [4]. It must also cover the measures to be taken if those risks materialize, including arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms [3]. The assessment applies to the first use of the high-risk AI system, though deployers may rely on previous assessments in similar cases [5]. If elements of the assessment change or become outdated during use, the deployer must update the information [5]. The AI Office may provide a template to facilitate compliance, which can include cross-references to data protection impact assessments [2].

Yes, deployers of high-risk AI systems must inform natural persons that they are subject to the use of such systems when making decisions or assisting in decisions related to them [1]. This obligation applies to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, which include systems used for recruitment, selection, and evaluating candidates in employment contexts [2]. However, this requirement does not apply to high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum where Union or national law considers the application disproportionate [3]. Additionally, the right to obtain clear explanations of the decision-making process applies to affected persons subject to decisions based on these systems, with specific exceptions for certain use cases [4]. The classification of an AI system as high-risk depends on whether it poses a significant risk of harm, including by materially influencing decision-making outcomes [5].

If a provider concludes that its Annex III AI system is not high-risk, it must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service [1]. The provider must also be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2) [1]. Upon request from national competent authorities, the provider must provide the documentation of its assessment [1]. If the market surveillance authority later finds the system is actually high-risk, the provider must take all necessary actions to bring it into compliance within a period prescribed by the authority [2]. If the provider fails to comply within that period, it will be subject to fines in accordance with Article 99 [3].

Yes, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner. This simplification applies provided that the SME does not have partner or linked enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC. The Commission is required to develop guidelines on these simplified elements without affecting the level of protection for high-risk AI systems. However, this simplified approach does not exempt SMEs from fulfilling other requirements laid down in the Regulation, including those in Articles 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 72, and 73.

Your employer is generally prohibited from using AI to infer your emotions at work unless the system is intended for medical or safety reasons [1]. If your employer does use such a high-risk emotion recognition system, they must inform you and your workers' representatives before putting it into service [2]. The Act defines an emotion recognition system as one that identifies or infers emotions based on biometric data [3]. Deployers of these systems must also inform you of their operation and ensure data processing follows specific regulations [4]. However, this prohibition does not apply if the system is permitted by law to detect, prevent, or investigate criminal offences with appropriate safeguards [4].

Yes, the use of AI systems for social scoring is prohibited. This ban applies to systems that evaluate or classify natural persons based on their social behaviour or known, inferred, or predicted personal characteristics. The prohibition specifically targets cases where the social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the data's origin or where such treatment is unjustified or disproportionate. This restriction covers the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of such systems [1].

No, it is not allowed to build a facial recognition database by scraping photos from the internet or CCTV footage. Article 5 explicitly prohibits the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage [1].

If the police start using real-time remote biometric identification in an emergency without prior authorisation, they must request it without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours [1]. If the authorisation is rejected, the use must be stopped immediately [1]. The request must be made by a judicial or independent administrative authority whose decision is binding [1]. This applies to the use of such systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement [1]. Member States must lay down detailed rules for these requests in their national law [5].

No, such an action does not count as manipulation for the purposes of the ban if it does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts. Article 5(1b) explicitly states that an AI system manipulating material in a way that fails to increase exposure of intimate parts shall not constitute manipulation. Consequently, the prohibition in Article 5(1)(ba) regarding the generation or manipulation of intimate parts without consent would not apply in this specific scenario. The definition of manipulation is narrowed by this exclusion to ensure only harmful manipulations are banned. Therefore, the AI photo editor's changes would fall outside the scope of the prohibited practices described. [1][2]

An AI system is considered high-risk if it is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment [1]. This classification applies regardless of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently [1]. However, a product required to undergo third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than those to health and safety, such as radio spectrum distribution, does not fulfill the condition for high-risk classification [3]. Additionally, AI systems listed in Annex III are considered high-risk independently of these product conditions [4]. If a provider believes an Annex III system is not high-risk, they must document their assessment before placing it on the market [5].

An AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes [1]. This exception applies specifically when the system performs a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task for Annex III use cases [1]. However, the system must always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons [1]. Additionally, the Commission can remove such systems from Annex III if they no longer pose significant risks and their deletion does not lower overall protection levels [2].

AI tools that detect cheating during exams are not automatically classified as high-risk if they meet specific conditions under Article 6. Such a system would not be considered high-risk if it is intended to detect decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, provided there is proper human review [1]. However, if the tool performs profiling of natural persons, it shall always be considered high-risk regardless of other factors [1]. The classification also depends on whether the system is deemed a safety component, which is determined by its use for safety-related aspects rather than just convenience or quality control [5]. Ultimately, the specific risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights determines the classification [1].

No, software that only organises the logistics of a political campaign is not considered a high-risk AI system.
This is because the Act explicitly excludes tools used to organise, optimise, or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view from the definition of high-risk AI systems intended to influence election outcomes.
[1]

Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs for a period of at least six months [1]. This duration applies unless applicable Union or national law, such as data protection laws, provides otherwise [1]. Financial institutions that are providers must maintain these logs as part of their internal governance documentation under Union financial services law [1]. Deployers of high-risk AI systems have the same obligation to keep logs for at least six months [2]. Financial institutions that are deployers must also maintain these logs as part of their relevant Union financial service law documentation [2].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs for a period of at least six months. This duration applies unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, particularly regarding personal data protection. Financial institutions that are deployers must maintain these logs as part of their internal governance documentation under Union financial services law. The requirement is found in Article 26(6) of the Act.

A provider must report a serious incident immediately after establishing a causal link or reasonable likelihood of such a link, but no later than 15 days after becoming aware of the incident [1]. If the incident involves the death of a person, the report must be made no later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident [2]. In cases of a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3, point (49)(b), the report must be provided no later than two days after becoming aware of the incident [4]. The period for reporting shall take account of the severity of the serious incident [1].

If a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system leads to a death, the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer establishes, or suspects, a causal relationship between the system and the incident. However, this report must not be later than 10 days after the date the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1]. This specific 10-day deadline applies notwithstanding the general reporting period found in other paragraphs of the same article [1][2]. The general reporting deadline for other serious incidents is 15 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the incident [2]. These rules apply to high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market [5].

Yes, providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so users are informed they are interacting with an AI system [1]. This obligation applies unless it is obvious from the user's perspective, or unless the system is authorized by law for criminal investigation purposes [1]. The rule does not apply if the chatbot is part of a system available for the public to report criminal offences [1]. There is no specific exemption mentioned for chatbots in the provided text beyond the general exceptions listed [1].

If you deploy an AI system that generates a deepfake video, you must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [1]. This obligation does not apply if the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence [1]. If the video forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work, the transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work [1]. The definition of a deepfake includes AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that would falsely appear to be authentic or truthful [2].

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation containing information from Annex XI for authorities [2]. They must also provide information and documentation to AI system integrators that includes elements from Annex XII [1]. Providers are required to cooperate with the Commission and national competent authorities [3]. They must implement a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including respecting reservations of rights under Directive (EU) 2019/790 [4]. Finally, they must draw up and make publicly available a detailed summary of the training content using a template from the AI Office [5].

The Commission can use the following criteria to determine if a general-purpose AI model has capabilities or impact equivalent to those set out in Article 51(1), point (a):
1. The number of parameters of the model [3].
2. The quality or size of the data set, for example measured through tokens [2].
3. The number of registered end-users [1].
4. The benchmarks and evaluations of capabilities, including adaptability, autonomy, and scalability [4].
5. The input and output modalities, such as text-to-text or text-to-image, along with state-of-the-art thresholds [5].

A model is presumed to have a high impact on the internal market if it has been made available to at least 10 000 registered business users established in the Union [1]. This presumption applies specifically when determining if the model meets the criteria for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 51 [1]. The regulation does not specify a different threshold for other types of users or impacts [4]. The definition of systemic risk includes risks propagated at scale across the value chain due to the model's reach [3]. High impact capabilities can also be presumed based on a cumulative computation threshold of greater than 10^25 floating point operations [2].

Yes, providers of general-purpose AI models must comply with copyright opt-outs. They are required to put in place a policy to identify and comply with reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [1]. This obligation applies specifically to general-purpose AI models under Chapter V of the Act [1]. The Act does not explicitly mention "opt-outs" by name in these passages, but it mandates compliance with such reservations of rights [1].

For SMEs, including start-ups, the maximum fine is the lower of the percentages or amounts specified in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99 [1]. This cap applies to fines referred to in those specific paragraphs [1]. The regulation also requires Member States to consider the economic viability of SMEs and start-ups when imposing penalties [2]. There is no separate maximum fine percentage or amount listed exclusively for start-ups distinct from SMEs in the provided text [1]. Therefore, the maximum fine for an SME and a start-up is determined by the same lower limit rule applied to SMEs [1].

The provided passages do not mention any specific relief, exemptions, or reduced fine structures for small or mid-cap companies. The fines listed are fixed amounts or percentages of worldwide turnover without distinguishing company size. [2][3][5] The text only states that fines are calculated based on the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, taking due account of proportionality and appropriateness. [5] No specific clause in these passages offers relief based on a company's market capitalization or size. [2][3][5]

Yes, you have the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system and the main elements of the decision taken. This right applies if the decision significantly affects your health, safety, or fundamental rights and is taken by a deployer based on a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III. However, this right does not apply if exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law. The explanation must be provided by the deployer to the affected person. [2]

Each EU country must ensure that at least one AI regulatory sandbox is operational by 2 August 2027 [1]. This obligation can also be fulfilled by participating in an existing sandbox that provides equivalent national coverage [1]. The European Data Protection Supervisor may establish a sandbox for Union institutions instead of a national one [2]. Member States are required to submit annual reports on the progress of these sandboxes starting from the year after their establishment [3]. The procedures for these sandboxes must be simple and uniformly recognized across the Union [5].

The provided passages do not specify a start date for when the high-risk rules apply to AI systems covered by product legislation in Annex I. They mention a deadline of 28 January 2028 for certain notified bodies to apply for designation [2], but this does not indicate when the rules themselves become effective. The text states that specific articles apply to high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation [1], yet it does not define the temporal commencement of this application. Consequently, the AI Act passages provided do not answer this question.
The AI Act applies in general from 2 August 2026. [5]

High-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before the date of application of Chapter III must comply only if they undergo significant changes in their designs as from that date [1]. Providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for public authorities must take necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2030 [1]. If a high-risk AI system has already been subject to a conformity assessment, it must undergo a new procedure if there is a substantial modification [3]. However, pre-determined changes to systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market do not constitute a substantial modification [3]. Distributors must also ensure systems are in conformity with requirements before making them available on the market [4].

A provider is not explicitly defined in the provided passages, but an operator is defined as including a provider [4]. A deployer is defined as a natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority, excluding personal non-professional activities [1]. The passages indicate that a deployer must assign human oversight to competent natural persons [3]. Deployers also have obligations that are without prejudice to other Union or national law [5]. The text does not explicitly state the difference between a provider and a deployer beyond the definition of a deployer.

The maximum fine for non-compliance with the prohibition of prohibited AI practices is up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher [1]. For Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, the fine for breaking such prohibitions is up to EUR 1 500 000 [2]. If a Union institution fails to meet other requirements or obligations under the Regulation besides Article 5, the fine is up to EUR 750 000 [3]. The passages do not specify a single maximum fine amount for general deployers breaking their obligations under Article 26, only that they must monitor operations and report incidents [4]. Therefore, a direct numerical comparison of maximum fines for a generic deployer breaking Article 26 obligations versus prohibited practices cannot be made from the provided text.

The provided passages do not state any fees or costs for registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database. They only describe the requirement to register before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [1][2]. The text mentions that the registration must include specific information and be stored in a secure section for certain systems [3], but it does not mention any monetary amount. Therefore, the AI Act passages provided do not answer this question.
